panels.title: Big questions
points: How can a poem be a recipe for a country?
What do the facts tell us about who lives in Britain today?
How can a poem help us see the world through someone else's eyes?
Can a poem keep hope alive when everything else seems lost?

panels.title: Islamic foundation
panels.text: Allah says that He made people into nations and tribes so that they may know one another, and that the most noble in His sight is the most righteous (al-Hujurat 49:13). Diversity is part of Allah's design; what matters is character, not origin.

panels.title: The British: identity, diversity and belonging
points: Benjamin Zephaniah (1958 to 2023), born in Birmingham
Poet, novelist and teacher of young writers
Wrote about fairness, race and being British
Performed poems aloud so everyone could enjoy them

panels.title: Non-fiction: Modern Britain, a diverse nation
points: Britain has welcomed newcomers for two thousand years
The 2021 Census counted everyone in England and Wales
Many languages are spoken in homes
Most people say English is their main language

panels.title: We Refugees: compassion and shared humanity
points: Forced to flee war, persecution or disaster
Protected by the 1951 Refugee Convention
UNHCR: over 100 million people forced from home (2023)
Most stay in neighbouring countries

panels.title: If I Must Die: hope, remembrance and legacy
points: Refaat Alareer (1979 to 2023), born in Gaza
Taught English literature and creative writing
Helped young people tell their stories in English

panels.title: Mother to Son: resilience and perseverance
points: Langston Hughes (1901 to 1967), American poet
Published Mother to Son in 1922
A mother speaks to her son
Her dialect makes the voice real and warm

panels.title: Whole-unit retrieval and poetry masterclass
points: retrieve a key quotation and method for each poem

plan a PETZAAL answer on one poem in five minutes

panels.title: How does Zephaniah present Britain in the ending?
points: Point: Zephaniah ends by showing how Britain should be treated
Evidence: 'Serve with justice / And enjoy.'
Technique: imperative verbs, the end of the recipe
Zoom in: 'justice' is an unusual thing to serve; it means fairness
Answer: Zephaniah ends with the imperatives 'Serve with justice / And enjoy', so the recipe becomes a rule for living: Britain is only complete when every ingredient is treated fairly.

panels.title: How does Zephaniah build empathy for refugees?
points: Point: Zephaniah makes readers see themselves in refugees
Evidence: 'We can all be refugees'
Technique: refrain and the inclusive pronoun 'we'
Zoom in: 'all' leaves no one out
Answer: Zephaniah builds empathy through the refrain 'We can all be refugees'; the inclusive pronoun 'we' and the word 'all' leave no reader outside the poem, so refugees stop being strangers.

panels.title: How does Alareer present legacy?
points: Point: Alareer presents legacy as hope passed to others
Evidence: 'let it bring hope / let it be a tale'
Technique: repetition of 'let it' (a plea)
Zoom in: 'tale' turns a death into a story
Answer: Alareer presents legacy as something given away: the repeated plea 'let it bring hope / let it be a tale' turns his possible death into a story that others will carry forward.

panels.title: How does Hughes present the mother's resilience?
points: Point: Hughes presents the mother as determined despite hardship
Evidence: 'Life for me ain't been no crystal stair.'
Technique: extended metaphor; dialect
Zoom in: 'crystal' suggests luxury she never had

Answer: Hughes presents the mother as resilient: 'Life for me ain't been no crystal stair' admits hardship plainly, and 'crystal' sets the luxury she never had against the worn stairs she still climbs.
